title: Consecutive edges detect cocones on a sequential infinity diagram
statement:
Use simplicial sets, nerves, quasicategories, coherent functor categories, mapping spaces, constant diagrams and colimits from [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $\mathbb N$ be the ordinary category with a unique arrow $a\to b$ if $a\leq b$. Let $L\subseteq N(\mathbb N)$ be the simplicial subset generated by all vertices and the edges $n\to n+1$ for $n\geq0$; its only nondegenerate simplices are these vertices and edges. For every quasicategory $\mathcal E$, restriction is an equivalence of quasicategories
$$\operatorname{Fun}(N(\mathbb N),\mathcal E)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal E).$$
For every coherent diagram $x:N(\mathbb N)\to\mathcal E$ and $t\in\mathcal E$, restriction therefore induces an equivalence
$$\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(N(\mathbb N),\mathcal E)}(x,\Delta t)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}_{\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal E)}(x|_L,\Delta t).$$
It is natural in $x,t$ and commutes with postcomposition by any coherent functor $\mathcal E\to\mathcal E'$ to a quasicategory $\mathcal E'$. A specified cocone on $x$ is colimiting if and only if its restriction to $L$ is colimiting. Neither existence of other colimits nor nonemptiness of $\mathcal E$ is assumed.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 4.4.2.6, printed p. 297, the inclusion of the consecutive-edge simplicial subset L into N(Z_{>=0}) is a categorical equivalence; its cocone consequence is used in Proposition 4.4.2.7. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/ (WANTED). No Stacks tag supplies this infinity-categorical statement.

proof.text: Write $B=N(\mathbb N)$ and $i:L\hookrightarrow B$. A simplex of $B$ is a weakly increasing sequence of natural numbers. Collapsing repeated entries factors it uniquely as a degeneracy of the strictly increasing sequence of its distinct entries. Thus nondegenerate simplices are precisely nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, with faces obtained by deleting entries. Write $\Delta^{[0,n]}$ for the full simplex on $0,\ldots,n$, and put $K_n=L\cup\Delta^{[0,n]}$. These are simplicial subsets, $K_0=K_1=L$, and $\bigcup_nK_n=B$: every finite increasing sequence has a finite largest entry. All these objects are small in any containing universe of the statement.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.2.6, printed p.297: explicit computation for the consecutive-edge inclusion; agent maximum-vertex filtration of its omitted computation.

proof.text: Fix $n\geq2$. The nondegenerate simplices of $K_n$ outside $K_{n-1}$ occur in pairs $(S,T)$, where $S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n\}$ contains $n-1,n$ and at least one smaller entry, and $T=S\setminus\{n-1\}$. Indeed, a new simplex contains $n$ and some entry at most $n-2$; it either contains $n-1$, giving $S$, or uniquely acquires it by insertion, giving $T$. Attach the finitely many $S$ in order of increasing dimension $r=|S|-1\geq2$, with arbitrary order among equal dimensions. All codimension-one faces of $S$ except $T$ are already present: deleting $n$ gives an old face, and deleting any entry other than $n-1,n$ leaves either the old edge $\{n-1,n\}$ or a smaller-dimensional $S$. Every proper face of $T$ is also present: deleting $n$ gives an old face; any other face is either the old vertex $\{n\}$ or is the paired face of a previously attached smaller-dimensional $S$. Neither $S$ nor $T$ was previously present. Equal-dimensional attachments have different missing faces because the pairing is injective. The intersection with the current subset is therefore exactly $\Lambda^r_{r-1}$ inside this $\Delta^r$, and $0<r-1<r$. The attachment is its pushout: on each degree maps glue uniquely on the union, and the resulting maps commute with operators because both given maps do and agree on the intersection. Unique collapse of repeated entries gives the same assertion for degenerate simplices. After these attachments all of $K_n$ is present.

source.place: Proof, normalized-simplex pairing and inner-horn pushout: agent variant using the final unit edge and the largest vertex, with all intersections proved here.

proof.text: Call a map an inner fibration if it lifts against every inner horn, and call a map inner anodyne if it has the left lifting property against every inner fibration. Each horn used in step 2 has that left lifting property by definition. Apply the pushout and finite-composition clauses of [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure] with the class of all inner fibrations to obtain the same property for $K_{n-1}\hookrightarrow K_n$. To pass to $B$, fix any square with $i:L\hookrightarrow B$ on the left and an inner fibration $p:X\to Y$ on the right. Start with its prescribed map on $K_1=L$. Given the lift on $K_{n-1}$, use the just-proved lifting property and the prescribed map $K_n\to B\to Y$ to choose a lift on $K_n$ agreeing exactly on $K_{n-1}$. Recursion and classical choice give compatible lifts for all $n$. Their union is a simplicial map $B\to X$: each simplex and each of its operators lie in one $K_n$, where the required identities hold. It solves the original square. This proves directly that $i$ is inner anodyne; no theorem about commuting arbitrary limits or colimits, and no transfinite-closure assertion beyond the cited statement, is used.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.2.6, printed p.297, missing computation; explicit lifting argument following the horn attachments of step 2.

proof.text:
Put $\mathcal D=\operatorname{Fun}(B,\mathcal E)$, $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Fun}(L,\mathcal E)$ and $q=i^*:\mathcal D\to\mathcal A$. By [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] these are quasicategories. We claim that $q$ has the right lifting property against every degreewise injective simplicial map $j:U\to V$. By the defining formula for $\operatorname{Fun}$, a square for $q$ and $j$ is exactly a map
$$(B\times U)\amalg_{L\times U}(L\times V)\longrightarrow\mathcal E.$$
The square's commutativity is exactly the agreement on $L\times U$. The map from this pushout to $B\times V$ is inner anodyne by [lem-coef-inner-anodyne-pushout-product], with $i$ as its inner-anodyne factor and $j$ its injective factor. Since $\mathcal E\to\Delta^0$ is an inner fibration by the quasicategory definition, the map extends to $B\times V$. Currying is the required lift. This includes $U=\varnothing$ and arbitrary $V$, not only positive-dimensional horn tests.

source.place: Corollaries 2.3.2.4 and 2.3.2.5, printed pp.100-101; the exponential lifting adjunction is written out using the existing pushout-product node.

proof.text: The lifting property in step 4 constructs a coherent quasi-inverse. Apply it to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow\mathcal A$ and the identity of $\mathcal A$ to obtain $s:\mathcal A\to\mathcal D$ with $qs=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal A}$. Let $J$ be the nerve of the ordinary category with two objects $0,1$ and exactly one morphism for each ordered pair of objects. Its two opposite edges are inverse, with the inverse equations witnessed by its two composition triangles. Apply step 4 to the degreewise injective inclusion $\{0,1\}\times\mathcal D\hookrightarrow J\times\mathcal D$. On its two components prescribe $\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal D}$ and $sq$; downstairs prescribe $q$ after projection $J\times\mathcal D\to\mathcal D$. The square commutes because $qsq=q$. A lift $H:J\times\mathcal D\to\mathcal D$ curries to $J\to\operatorname{Fun}(\mathcal D,\mathcal D)$. This target is a quasicategory by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. The two opposite edges and their composition triangles map to inverse coherent transformations between $\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal D}$ and $sq$, hence give a coherent natural equivalence by the definition in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Together with $qs=\mathrm{id}$ this proves that the specified restriction $q$ is a functor equivalence. The argument also works when $\mathcal E$ is empty: then $\mathcal A=\mathcal D=\varnothing$, and all displayed lifting problems still make sense.

source.place: Corollary 2.3.2.5, printed p.101, trivial-fibration conclusion; explicit section and inverse-triangle argument for the coherent-equivalence convention of this DAG.

proof.text: A functor equivalence induces equivalences on every mapping space by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus]. Apply this to $q$ and the objects $x,\Delta_Bt$. Restriction of a constant diagram is exactly constant: $q\Delta_Bt=\Delta_Lt$, since both simplicial maps factor through the same $t$ and the unique map to $\Delta^0$. Thus the resulting map on mapping spaces is exactly the restriction map in the statement. Its naturality is that of the specified simplicial functor $q$, without choosing an inverse to a comparison map. More explicitly, a simplex $h:B\times\Delta^m\to\mathcal E$ restricts to $h\circ(i\times\mathrm{id})$; this operation commutes with every simplex operator and restricts all coherent transformations and their composition witnesses as well. Consequently it commutes with precomposition in $x$ and postcomposition in the constant target, including their coherence simplices. For an enhanced functor $G:\mathcal E\to\mathcal E'$, the equality $G\circ h\circ(i\times\mathrm{id})=(G\circ h)\circ(i\times\mathrm{id})$ holds degree by degree. Applying this also to the simplices of the pinched mapping-space definition proves the claimed compatibility with postcomposition by $G$.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.2.6, printed p.297, cocone consequence of its categorical equivalence; mapping-space and naturality details supplied by the existing enhanced calculus.

proof.text:
Let $\lambda:x\to\Delta_Bc$ be the specified cocone. The cocone criterion (the dual clause) of [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus] says it is colimiting exactly when, for every $t\in\mathcal E$, the map
$$\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal E}(c,t)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal D}(x,\Delta_Bt),\qquad a\longmapsto\Delta_B(a)\circ\lambda$$
is an equivalence. The same criterion for $q\lambda$ has target $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathcal A}(x|_L,\Delta_Lt)$. Its map is the previous one followed by the restriction equivalence from step 6, with the compatibility homotopy supplied by restriction of the composition witnesses; constants restrict exactly as shown there. Composing a map of spaces with an equivalence does not change whether it is an equivalence: on components it composes with a bijection, and on every based homotopy group with an isomorphism, so these cancel in either direction. Thus the two cocone criteria agree for each $t$, proving both implications for this particular cocone. This uses no existence of other colimits.

lean.statement: theorem infinity_sequential_spine (E : SSet.{u}) [Quasicategory E] : IsFunctorEquivalence (sequentialRestriction E) ∧ (∀ (x : ((ihom sequentialNerve.{u}).obj E) _⦋0⦌) (t : E _⦋0⦌), IsWeakHomotopyEquivalence (mappingSpaceMap (sequentialRestriction E) x ((constantDiagrams sequentialNerve.{u} E).app _ t))) ∧ constantDiagrams sequentialNerve.{u} E ≫ sequentialRestriction E = constantDiagrams sequentialSpine.toSSet E ∧ (∀ (T : SSet.{u}) (H : T ⟶ (ihom sequentialNerve.{u}).obj E), MonoidalClosed.uncurry (H ≫ sequentialRestriction E) = (sequentialSpine.ι ▷ T) ≫ MonoidalClosed.uncurry H) ∧ (∀ (E' : SSet.{u}) [Quasicategory E'] (G : E ⟶ E'), sequentialRestriction E ≫ (ihom sequentialSpine.toSSet).map G = (ihom sequentialNerve.{u}).map G ≫ sequentialRestriction E') ∧ (∀ F : sequentialNerve.{u} ⟶ E, ∃ R : coconeCategory F ⟶ coconeCategory (sequentialSpine.ι ≫ F), (∀ (n : SimplexCategoryᵒᵖ) (c : (coconeCategory F).obj n), (R.app n c).1.1 = c.1.1 ∧ (R.app n c).1.2 = ((ihom Δ[1]).map (sequentialRestriction E)).app n c.1.2) ∧ ∀ c : (coconeCategory F) _⦋0⦌, IsColimiting F c ↔ IsColimiting (sequentialSpine.ι ≫ F) (R.app _ c))
